title: Redwood POC weekly sync - Quantaco AI - cost econ
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on cost/unit economics. Reviewed tokens/sec/$ benchmarks across hosted vs dedicated configs, caching and batching tradeoffs, and immediate tuning items. Agreement to run a 1M-token burst benchmark with updated caching settings and to share a refreshed cost model spreadsheet. Action: Redwood to provision test run, Quantaco to provide production trace sample.
topics: cost per token and tokens/sec/$ benchmarking
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Alright folks welcome back to the weekly P O C sync with Quantaco, um it's Jordan and Priya from Redwood. Thanks for joining.
[00:06] Carlos Mendes: Yeah hi thanks, morning everyone. We have a short agenda: cost review, the tuning we did last week, and then next steps for the benchmark.
[00:12] Priya Patel: Quick note — we pushed the new caching config to the sandbox and ran the prefix-heavy simulation you sent. Wanted to show the numbers up front.
[00:20] Aisha Khan: Great, that's the one with long prompt chains and lots of repeated system prompt tokens, correct?
[00:24] Priya Patel: Yep, exactly. So high level: baseline hosted run (no caching, conservative batching) gave us about ~1,100 tokens/sec per dollar. With KV/prefix caching enabled and more aggressive dynamic batching we saw 3,300 tokens/sec per dollar — roughly 3x improvement.
[00:40] Ben Cho: Wait can you repeat the units? tokens per second per dollar?
[00:44] Priya Patel: Sorry, tokens per second per dollar, shorthand tokens/sec/$. It's our internal metric for throughput normalized by cost. So higher is better for throughput economics.
[00:52] Carlos Mendes: That 3x is with what latency? Our 95th is important.
[00:56] Priya Patel: Right — tail latencies moved a bit. Baseline median CPU was around 120ms per chunk, 95th was ~450ms. With batching increased to group size ~64 and caching on, median stayed ~140ms, but 95th rose to ~580ms in the saturated scenario. For most of your interactive flows 95th under the caching config was under 500ms; the higher number came from sustained burst at high concurrency.
[01:20] Maya Li: So there's a tradeoff — more throughput per dollar but a tail hit. How much of your workloads are prefix re-useable? If it's mostly repeated system prompts we get big wins from cache.
[01:30] Priya Patel: From your trace sample we saw about 48% prefix reuse within a rolling 10-minute window. That translated to around 45-55% token cost savings purely from KV cache for that trace.
[01:41] Carlos Mendes: Those are good numbers. Did you test quantization or smaller model variants for price comps?
[01:47] Jordan Lee: We ran a comparison across three model variants: rdm-13b (float16), rdm-13b-8q (8-bit quant), and a smaller 7b. Cost econ wise the 8-bit quant gave approx 1.4x better tokens/sec/$ versus float16 for the same config, but quality delta was small on your sample prompts. The 7b cut cost further but we saw regression on longer reasoning chains.
[02:08] Ben Cho: Any note about dedicated vs hosted pricing? We're trying to understand when to commit to reserved capacity.
[02:12] Priya Patel: Sure — quick summary: hosted is simpler and has no commit but unit cost is higher. Dedicated reserved capacity (monthly commit) can drop unit cost by ~25-40% depending on instance type and utilization. The break-even point from your expected Q3 volume was projected around 600M tokens/month in our spreadsheet. We'll share the updated model with the commit sensitivity table.
[02:33] Aisha Khan: On security questions — SOC2 and key management. If we go dedicated/on-prem what K M S options do we have?
[02:39] Jordan Lee: For Dedicated we support customer-managed keys via AWS KMS or external HSM integrations for on-prem. We also provide audit logs and RBAC. We'll attach the security pack and SOC2 artifact in the follow-up.
[02:49] Carlos Mendes: Great. Back to batching: you said dynamic batching — can you explain how that affects latency for small requests vs large?
[02:56] Priya Patel: Dynamic batching tries to accumulate compatible requests for a short window (e.g., 10-20ms) to increase GPU utilization. For short-turn requests that are latency-sensitive we lower the batch window and prefer cache hits. In our sandbox tests, a 10ms window vs 30ms window gave about 20% lower throughput but 30-40% better median latency.
[03:18] Ben Cho: So we can tune per-route? Like keep chat endpoints low-latency, bulk generation endpoints optimized for cost?
[03:22] Priya Patel: Exactly — per-route policies are supported. You can pin latency SLOs and Redwood routes traffic accordingly, fallback to another variant if SLOs can't be met.
[03:31] Maya Li: We noticed some odd tokenization artifacts in the transcript last week — some names got munged. Anything we should know about tokenizer configs when switching models?
[03:38] Priya Patel: Tokenizer differences can cause visible changes for edge cases, especially if you switch model families. We recommend running a small eval prompt set across candidate models to surface differences. We'll include a tokenizer check in the benchmark run.
[03:49] Carlos Mendes: About caching savings — are those savings linear with reuse rate? Like if we go from 48% reuse to 60% reuse do we get 25% more savings?
[03:56] Priya Patel: It's not perfectly linear because cache hits reduce generation compute but batching and memory pressure introduce diminishing returns. Rough rule: each 10pp increase in reuse gave us ~8-10% incremental tokens/sec/$ improvement in our sims, until cache pressure starts to evict useful entries.
[04:12] Jordan Lee: Also worth noting network egress and storage for cache state add small infra costs; we account for that in the cost model.
[04:19] Ben Cho: Competitor question — did you test the same trace on any managed provider for apples-to-apples?
[04:24] Priya Patel: We did a rough comparison with one managed endpoint (Vendor X) using their published perf numbers and your trace. Redwood's optimized runtime with caching gave about ~2.5x tokens/sec/$ better in that head-to-head for this workload. We'll mark vendor names in the spreadsheet.
[04:38] Carlos Mendes: Good. What's the proposed test for next week?
[04:41] Jordan Lee: Action plan: Redwood to run a 1M-token burst test in a dedicated sandbox with updated caching settings + 8-bit quant variant, measure tokens/sec/$, median/95th latencies, and cache hit rate. Quantaco to provide a 24-hour prod trace sample (PII sanitized) to seed realistic request distribution. We'll also run a route-level latency SLO test.
[05:01] Aisha Khan: Timeline?
[05:03] Jordan Lee: We'll spin up the test by Thursday, run it Friday, and share results Monday. If we need to demo config changes live we'll schedule a 30-minute deep-dive next Tuesday.
[05:13] Ben Cho: Anything else from the team?
[05:15] Maya Li: I'd like us to validate failover — what happens to requests if dedicated pool is saturated? Does Redwood fallback to hosted?
[05:22] Priya Patel: Yes we can configure automated fallback policies to a compatible model in hosted or another region. We'll include failure-mode tests in the benchmark.
[05:30] Carlos Mendes: Awesome, thanks. Quick recap of next steps?
[05:33] Jordan Lee: Sure: 1) Redwood to share updated cost model spreadsheet and the vendor comparison, 2) Quantaco to send sanitized 24-hour trace, 3) Redwood to run 1M-token benchmark (dedicated sandbox, caching on, 8-bit quant) and share results, 4) schedule deep-dive if results require config tuning.
[05:52] Ben Cho: Sounds good.
[05:53] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links to the artifacts (spreadsheet, security pack, and test run link). End call.
